extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of advertising history; general readers interested in 18th-century social history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and exemplifying the features, formats, and rhetorical strategies used in 18th-century newspaper advertisements and notices (e.g., boxing challenges, market agents, quack cures, marriage notices, rewards, literary promotions). Useful for analyzing how ads were composed, what information they included, and the social functions they served.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boxing-match/challenge advertisement format
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements for boxing matches present rival statements by each contestant, state the stake, the rules or terms, the precise time and venue, and mention attendance/diversions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from text: challenger (Ann Field) states her local standing and invites Mrs. Stokes to a trial for 10 pounds, 'fair rise and fall'; the championess (Elizabeth Stokes) replies with past victory and agrees to meet for the said sum; notice includes attendance time: 'Attendance will be given at one, and the encounter to begin at four precisely.' Also mentions accompanying diversions ('cudgel-playing'). Use: to declare claims, set terms, mobilize spectators, and add spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise sale-of-person (slave) advertisement structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Very short notice specifying the human commodity, age, and a place to inquire (e.g., 'To be sold, a Negro boy, aged eleven years. Enquire of the Virginia Coffee-house in Threadneedle street').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how human trafficking was advertised tersely: object (Negro boy) + age + inquiry location; no further detail or moral mitigation. Useful for recognizing minimal factual inventory and dehumanizing commerce in period ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-spectacle / animal-baiting advert attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices for spectacles (cock-matches, bull-baiting) specify the event type, sometimes duration ('last the week'), sensational practices (use of fireworks), and are framed to excite an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to promote brutal/entertaining spectacles by advertising scope and sensational elements. Indicates that cruelty and excitement were overt selling points in public entertainment notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent/service advertisement (estate/financial agent) conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Classified-style ads list types of business wanted or offered (wants to buy estates, wants to sell, raise money), invite inquiries to a named agent, state terms (will answer letters post-paid, will advertise if desired), and give detailed attendance schedule and meeting places (coffee-houses and times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mr Thomas Rogers lists 'Estates which some Persons want to Buy/Sell', promises particulars via himself, 'answers letters Post-paid', and gives daily times and locations (Essex Street, Rainbow Coffee-house, Tom's, Will's). Guidance: agents advertise scope of service, contact logistics, and payment/advertising terms to reassure clients and structure meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service-legitimacy / credential-and-price assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Providers of disputed/socially-sensitive services (e.g., Fleet marriage parsons) assert authority/credentials and explicitly state pricing policy to counter accusations of imposition (e.g., 'Marriages are performed by authority by the Rev. Mr. Symson... N.B. — Without imposition').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such phrasing seeks to reassure clients about legality and fair charging. Use in ads to counter contemporaneous suspicions about clandestine or exploitative practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public apology / retraction advertisement form
rubrics_metrics.description: A printed confession/apology sets out the false statement, declares its untruth, expresses regret, and often appends witnesses' names to vindicate the person wronged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Joseph Robins' full apology admitting he never knew the alleged practice and asking pardon. Function: public redress of reputation through the press; template for formal retractions and libel settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge/duel / 'satisfaction of a gentleman' notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices responding to assaults or satires call for 'a meeting' to provide 'satisfaction', instruct how accused parties should reply (e.g., leave a line at a specified coffee-house), and sometimes limit engagement conditions (single opponent, time/place).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects the ritualized code of honor: ads serve as formal public calls-to-arms or requests for redress and specify neutral channels (coffee-houses) for arranging a duel/meeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward-and-recovery advertisement pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewards specify the item sought (often live), the exact reward amount, clear delivery instructions (addresses or persons), deadlines, and explicit exclusions or conditions (e.g., 'It must not be a Swallow, Swift or Martin that has been kept in a cage').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ten Guineas for delivering a live swallow to Thomas Meysey before a date; includes alternatives for delivery and reimbursement of travel. Such ads provide precise logistics and conditions to avoid disputes and to encourage recovery efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quack medical device / health-product advertisement tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Health-product ads claim efficacy, cite notable patrons or distinguished users, invite trials by 'Ladies and Gentlemen', and assert special benefits (e.g., suitability for children).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Henry Marsh's 'Chamber Horse' ad claims relief for a specific ailment, names persons of distinction as clients, and asks the public to try the device. Tactic: combine anecdotal testimony, novelty, and experiential invitation to sell questionable remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pest-expert / remedy advertisement features
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims succession to an authoritative practitioner, references to a published treatise with scholarly approbation, promises immediate diagnosis ('at the first sight will justly tell which of their beds are infested'), offers economical terms and DIY remedy options ('may be furnish'd with the Non Pareil Liquor').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mary Southall positions herself as successor to John Southall (author of Treatise of Bugs), emphasizes Royal Society approbation, offers both service and do-it-yourself remedies. Strategy: combine scholarly authority, guarantees, and tiered service/pricing to capture different client segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book / literary advertisement components
rubrics_metrics.description: Book ads give title, price, a short description or claim about contents and importance ('The many notorious Falsehoods... are all expos'd'), publisher and place, and often list other available works; sometimes include endorsement quotes or classical allusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'AN APOLOGY for the LIFE of Mrs. Shamela Andrews' — price, content summary, publisher 'Printed for A. Dodd', and two other titles listed. Function: inform buyers of content/value and cross-promote inventory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/gimmick promotions (prints + lotteries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shop or product promotions pair novelty publications or goods with lotteries or games of chance (e.g., 'Lottery For Husbands for young Maids'), promise that 'Not one Blank, but All Prizes', use engraved prints as enticement, and offer free samples or give-aways at a named shop with precise signage instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Interpretation of Women's Dreams includes engraved prints and a lottery with guaranteed prizes; distribution details: 'Given Gratis at Mr Burchell's Anodyne Necklace Shop... sign of the case of knives next shop to Drury Lane.' Tactic: combine spectacle, perceived value, and immediate retail location cues to drive foot traffic and sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal/romantic notice conventions (anonymity and instructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal notices describe the observed person and request anonymous or indirect contact via public houses/coffee-houses or by leaving letters directed to initials (e.g., 'send him directions... to be left for P. M. Z. at the Portugal Coffee house').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to solicit correspondence or meetings while preserving discretion; gives clear instructions for how the desired party should reply and where to leave communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-club / event notice format (meetings of 'Bloods')
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcements for private social gatherings state the assembled group name, venue (house name), organizer, purpose (entertainment), and punctuality/instructions for dining (e.g., 'Dinner will be on the Table punctually at two o'clock').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: coordinate membership events, emphasize exclusivity and punctual social ritual; provide precise logistics to ensure attendance and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humour, satire and sensational language as advert strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Many advertisements and notices employ humour, burlesque, satire, and sensational or indelicate descriptions to attract attention (e.g., ridicule of 'ass-driver', mocking boast about 'the blows... more difficult to digest than any she ever gave her asses', burlesques of 'Pamela').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text shows advertisers and pamphleteers exploited wit, mockery, and sensationalism to make announcements memorable and increase sales or readership; recognize rhetorical play as a deliberate attention-getting device.
